body:
You are drafting DIALOGUE TEXT for a video game. Reply in plain text only, in exactly the format asked at the end.

"The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG (think Baldur's Gate 3: fully voiced, branching dialogue, skill checks, a storyteller Narrator). It is folk horror set in Druskenvald, an afterlife realm of endless night under a gargantuan crescent moon with a leering crone's face; an autumn that never ends, pumpkins and bonfires and dead leaves everywhere, but the stakes are real. Humour is deadpan and sits beside the dread. Use only the names given here; invent no new named people, places, monsters or history.

THE PARTY: the player leads four heroes; never name, describe or gender the player's heroes. Some of the party may be these companions, who speak only in the `interject` lines written for them (each line is said only if that companion is present, so it must make sense on its own and never answer another companion's line):
- rook_coldwake: Rook, a Graveborn (undead) fighter, a graveyard rest warden; dry, level, practical, union-minded, cares that the dead are laid to rest properly; few words.
- tobin_hayward: Tobin, a Harvestborn (living scarecrow of wicker and straw) druid; brisk, warm, country-wise, talks about rot, roots, harvests and neighbours; kind under the sharp tongue.
- silas_vane: Silas, a Relicborn (skeleton-folk) monk and card sharp from river landings; fast, cocky, thinks in odds, bets and marks.
- delphine_ravelle: Delphine, a Threadborn (living patchwork doll) warlock; theatrical vaudeville showwoman, says "darling", treats horror as a third-rate sideshow she means to headline.
- lucan_houndstooth: Lucan, a Curseborn (wolf-man) ranger and monster hunter; hushed and earnest, narrates danger like a nature broadcaster, notices scents and tracks.
- cordelia_skein: Cordelia, a Silkborn (spider-folk) sorcerer; cool, cultivated, clinical, delighted by anything morbid as a subject of study.

RULES FOR THE TEXT
- Spoken lines: 1 to 3 short sentences, about 12 to 30 words, never over 40. Contractions are normal. People talk in their own voice and do not explain the plot to the audience. Accent is word choice and rhythm, never phonetic spelling. Country folk of the Hollow speak with a folksy country drawl in their word choice.
- Interject lines: one sentence, under 20 words.
- Option lines (what the player's party says or does): under 12 words, plain, in the party's voice ("We..." or an imperative).
- Narrator lines (the Vagrant, an old train conductor telling the tale afterwards: warm, folksy, wry, a Southern drawl in word choice such as reckon, ain't, folks, a spell, a piece; drop a final g in at most one line in three): second person, present tense, one or two sentences, only what a hero could perceive, concrete senses (smell, sound, texture, cold), no game words (HP, roll, level, check, DC, save, hit points), never tell the player what to feel, never the word "suddenly", never mention a fiddle, never name the Vagrant.
- No stage directions, asterisks, italics, brackets, placeholders, emoji or em dashes (use commas, periods, colons). Straight quotes only. Do not use the arrow characters -> or => inside the text.
- Content is dark but restrained: no gore, no graphic detail.
- Each brief says what the line must do; keep its facts, write it as the speaker would say it.

THIS SCENE: the villain's appearances between the chapters, on the roads of Wickermoor Hollow and at the party's campfire.

THE CROOKED MAN (speaker id crooked_man): the shade of the old master of a haunted manor, long dead; tall, lanky, limbs at wrong angles, a hanged man's neck, a tattered suit, a bent top hat low over his eyes, a huge yellow grin. He is the chief servant of the Crooked Queen (call her "the Queen" or "she"; never any other name), who is imprisoned and wants to wake. He is a SHOWMAN: warm, unhurried, theatrical, courteous to the point of menace, delighted with "my dears". He HINTS and NEVER EXPLAINS: every answer is a compliment, a riddle or a promise that sounds like a threat. He never raises his voice. He is never a fight: a blade passes through him. He speaks in complete, elegant sentences. Do NOT hint at any weakness of his.

What the story allows him to know and say (and nothing more): six powerful villains called the Fallen must die for the Queen's ritual (he calls them candles); the heroes have been killing them one by one out of goodness, which is exactly what the Queen wants; the party has cleared his old manor, the Crooked House, where a hag he calls "the lady upstairs" lived; the village of Wickermoor will hold a festival called Fool's Day; Lord Phillip and Lady Adela Druskenvald, the party's hosts at the manor, are part of the Queen's plan; Lady Adela has prophetic dreams. The Fallen, in the order the lines name them: a scarecrow terror at Foxwillow, a red abbot at a mountain monastery, Mister Crossroads the gambler at the Drowned Crossroads, a weeping Matron at a sanatorium by a lake, and a sixth under the fog at Maidenmist cemetery.

The lines marked "(the note)" are the words of a letter he left, which read themselves aloud in his voice: write them as his written words, in his voice.

The scenes (the [[n]] markers in this file are yours; everything else is fixed):

```
# --- Five of six: a note on the signpost ---

~ note
if flag.cm_note_read
-> END
endif
set cm_note_read
Narrator: [[36]]
Narrator: [[37]]
crooked_man [smile]: [[38]]
crooked_man [sly]: [[39]]
interject name:silas_vane: [[40]]
* [[41]] -> nt_burn
* [[42]] -> nt_keep

~ nt_burn
Narrator: [[43]]
-> END

~ nt_keep
Narrator: [[44]]
-> END

# --- Four of six: a guest at the fire (a night event) ---

~ fire
set cm_fire_met
appear crooked_man
Narrator: [[45]]
crooked_man [smile]: [[46]]
crooked_man [sly]: [[47]]
interject name:tobin_hayward: [[48]]
interject name:delphine_ravelle: [[49]]
* [[50]] -> cf_six
* [[51]] -> cf_couple
* [if flag.road_hair_given] [[52]] -> cf_hair
* [[53]] -> cf_throw
* [[54]] -> cf_leave

~ cf_six
crooked_man [smile]: [[55]]
crooked_man [sly]: [[56]]
-> cf_go

~ cf_couple
crooked_man [sly]: [[57]]
-> cf_go

~ cf_hair
crooked_man [smile]: [[58]]
-> cf_go

~ cf_throw
Narrator: [[59]]
crooked_man [smile]: [[60]]
-> cf_go

~ cf_leave
crooked_man [smile]: [[61]]
-> cf_go

~ cf_go
crooked_man [smile]: [[62]]
vanish crooked_man
Narrator: [[63]]
-> END

# --- Six of six: the last visit before Fool's Day (a night event) ---

~ last_fire
set cm_last_fire_met
appear crooked_man
Narrator: [[64]]
crooked_man [sad]: [[65]]
crooked_man [smile]: [[66]]
interject name:rook_coldwake: [[67]]
interject name:cordelia_skein: [[68]]
* [[69]] -> lf_defy
* [[70]] -> lf_couple
* [[71]] -> lf_silent

~ lf_defy
crooked_man [smile]: [[72]]
approve rook_coldwake +1 tobin_hayward +1 lucan_houndstooth +1: You told the Crooked Man to his face that you would stop him
-> lf_go

~ lf_couple
crooked_man [sly]: [[73]]
-> lf_go

~ lf_silent
crooked_man [smile]: [[74]]
-> lf_go

~ lf_go
crooked_man [smile]: [[75]]
vanish crooked_man
Narrator: [[76]]
-> END
```

Briefs for the markers:
36. narrator: a note is nailed to the snapped signpost at the crossing with a rusty nail, addressed in a looping, theatrical hand to "the heroes of the Hollow"
37. narrator: as you unfold it, the words read themselves aloud in a voice you know, warm and unhurried, from somewhere behind your left ear
38. crooked_man: (the note) five of six, my dears; only one candle left now, burning under the fog at Maidenmist; he is sure they will find it
39. crooked_man: (the note) and when it is out, Wickermoor will hold a festival, Fool's Day; he has reserved them the very best seats, in the front row
40. interject silas_vane: a man who saves you the front row wants you where he can see your face; I've done it myself
41. option: burn the note
42. option: keep the note
43. narrator: it burns green and quick and smells of the bone bonfire at the crossing, and the ash blows uphill against the wind
44. narrator: you fold it away, and all the way down the road it's warm in your pocket, the way a sleeping animal is warm
45. narrator: the one on watch looks up from the fire and he is sitting across it, knees up round his ears, warming long hands that cast no shadow on the ground
46. crooked_man: forgive the hour, my dears; a host must call on his guests now and then, and the fire looked so very welcoming
47. crooked_man: four of six; that makes it the interval, does it not; everyone stretch their legs before the second act
48. interject tobin_hayward: the fire's gone cold on his side; look at the frost on the logs
49. interject delphine_ravelle: an interval and no bar; darling, what sort of theatre are you running
50. option: ask what happens when all six are gone
51. option: ask about Phillip and Adela
52. option: ask for our hair back
53. option: throw a burning stick at him
54. option: tell him to leave our fire
55. crooked_man: a party, naturally; the whole valley is invited, and the guest of honour has been waiting a very long time
56. crooked_man: he would never spoil the surprise; that would be unforgivably rude
57. crooked_man: the Lord and Lady are well, for now; Lady Adela dreams so beautifully, and he has been reading her dreams over her shoulder
58. crooked_man: oh, it is quite safe; it has been woven into something lovely; they will see it when the time comes
59. narrator: the stick goes through him and lands in the frost on his side of the fire, and it goes out with a hiss
60. crooked_man: he laughs, delighted; such spirit; that is exactly why he likes them
61. crooked_man: of course; a guest should never overstay, and neither should a host
62. crooked_man: goodnight, my dears; sleep well, the road is long and the second act is the better one
63. narrator: the fire flares blue and then it's only a fire again, but the cold he left in the ground stays a good hour
64. narrator: he is there again in the small hours, standing behind the one on watch with his hat held to his chest like a mourner at a graveside
65. crooked_man: all six, my dears; every candle; she is awake now, and she asked him to say thank you, from the bottom of her heart
66. crooked_man: Fool's Day comes to Wickermoor soon; there will be dancing and a parade, and the Lord and Lady will have the best seats of all
67. interject rook_coldwake: he talks like an undertaker taking orders; I know the type
68. interject cordelia_skein: thanking us; how very precise of him; I find I would rather be cursed
69. option: tell him we'll stop whatever comes next
70. option: ask what she wants with Phillip and Adela
71. option: say nothing
72. crooked_man: he applauds softly; that is exactly what he is counting on; he has never once been disappointed in them
73. crooked_man: every good story ends with a wedding or a fire, and he has always preferred to have both
74. crooked_man: he nods, appreciative; a silent audience is the best kind
75. crooked_man: the curtain goes up very soon; do not be late
76. narrator: by morning there are footprints all round the fire, long and narrow, and every one of them points backwards

## Reply format
One line per marker, in order, exactly `n => text` (no quotes around the text, no extra lines, no commentary). 41 lines, numbered as above.
result:
36 => Somebody's gone and nailed a scrap of parchment to the busted signpost with a rusted iron spike. It's addressed to "the heroes of the Hollow" in a tall, looping hand.
37 => Soon as you unfold the paper, the ink starts talkin' right behind your left ear, warm and slow like an old friend leaning in.
38 => Five of six, my dears, and only one little candle left burning beneath the fog at Maidenmist. I have every confidence you shall snuff it out before long.
39 => Once the dark is complete, Wickermoor shall hold its grand Fool's Day festival. I have taken the liberty of reserving you the very finest seats in the front row.
40 => Any man who saves you the front row just wants your face where he can watch it, trust me.
41 => Burn the note in the road.
42 => Fold the note and keep it.
43 => The paper catches in a quick green flare that reeks of scorched bone from the crossing, and the grey ash drifts uphill against the wind.
44 => You tuck the parchment into your coat, and for a good long piece down the road it stays warm against your ribs like a sleeping hound.
45 => Whoever's keeping watch looks up through the smoke to find him perched across the embers, long knees drawn up by his ears and pale hands casting no shadow on the dirt.
46 => Do forgive the late hour, my dears. A proper host must look in on his guests now and again, and your fire looked so terribly inviting from the road.
47 => Four of six are done, which brings us neatly to the interval, does it not? Do stretch your legs and catch your breath before the second act begins.
48 => The fire's gone dead cold on his side of the ring, and there's white frost creeping up the logs.
49 => An interval without a bar is a crime, darling, so tell me what sort of third-rate theatre you are running.
50 => What happens when all six candles are out?
51 => Tell us how Lord Phillip and Lady Adela are faring.
52 => Give us back the hair we traded on the road.
53 => Hurl a burning branch straight at his grin.
54 => Get away from our camp and leave us be.
55 => Why, a celebration, naturally. The entire valley is invited to the gala, and our guest of honour has been waiting in the dark for a very long time.
56 => I would never dream of spoiling the surprise before the curtain rises, my dears. That would be unforgivably rude of me.
57 => The good Lord and Lady are quite well, for the moment. Dear Lady Adela dreams such exquisite things, and I have been reading every vision right over her shoulder.
58 => Oh, your little keepsake is quite safe, I assure you. It has been woven into something truly lovely, and you shall admire the craftsmanship when the hour arrives.
59 => The blazing branch sails clean through his coat without catching, lands in the white frost behind him, and dies with a wet hiss.
60 => Oh, well struck, my dears! Such marvellous spirit is precisely why you remain my very favourite company.
61 => Of course, forgive my imposition. A polite guest knows better than to overstay his welcome, and so does a host.
62 => Goodnight to you, my dears. Rest easy while you may, for the road ahead is long and the second act is by far the finer one.
63 => The flames snap blue for the space of a breath before settlin' back to orange, though the frost in the dirt takes a good hour to thaw.
64 => In the small, dead hours before dawn, he's standing right behind the night watch, holding his bent top hat against his ribs like a mourner by an open grave.
65 => All six are out at last, my dears, every single candle. She is awake in the dark now, and she asked me to thank you from the very bottom of her heart.
66 => Fool's Day comes to Wickermoor very soon now. There will be music and a grand parade, and the good Lord and Lady shall have the finest seats in the house.
67 => He talks just like an undertaker measuring a box before the body's even cold, and I know the breed.
68 => Being thanked so politely by a shade is fascinating, though I believe I would much rather have been cursed.
69 => We will stop whatever you and your Queen have planned.
70 => What does your Queen want with Phillip and Adela?
71 => Say nothing and let him speak.
72 => Bravo, my dears, bravo. That fierce resolve is precisely what I am counting on, and you have never once disappointed me.
73 => Every truly memorable tale concludes with either a wedding or a roaring fire, my dears. I have always preferred to arrange for both.
74 => How wonderfully poised you are tonight. A hushed audience is always the most attentive kind, my dears.
75 => The curtain rises on Wickermoor very soon now, my dears. Do make sure you are not late for your cue.
76 => Come morning, the cold ash is ringed with long, narrow footprints pressed deep into the frost, and every last one of them points backwards.
